processing: Black tea or tea powder boiled with milk, sugar and often ginger and cardamom, then strained and served as a small half serving in a glass.
harvest_season: Not relevant: it is a roadside serving made from everyday black tea.
appearance_dry: Not sold as a distinct dry tea; street chai usually starts from small granular black tea.
appearance_liquor: Opaque, deep tan milk tea in a small glass.
appearance_wet: Not applicable: it is strained on pouring.
taste_profile: Hot, sweet and milky, with ginger and spice around the tea.

brewing.notes: Boil tea powder with water, ginger and spices, add milk and sugar, strain, and fill a small glass only partway.

vintage_note: Sold by the glass at street stalls, never by year or season. The tea behind it is an everyday black tea bought for current use.
description:
Cutting chai is less a tea than a way of ordering one: a half glass of strong chai from a Mumbai roadside stall. The word means the full cup has been cut in half, at a lower price.

It is a milk tea boiled with sugar and, in many versions, ginger and cardamom.

It is hot and sweet, gone in a few mouthfuls. Small glasses matter, because this drink is built for a quick stop.

There is nothing to look for on a shelf. In Mumbai, pick a busy stall and have it with a vada pav before a local train, which is the classic setting.
history:
Cutting chai belongs to Mumbai's street stalls. The usual explanation of the name is that vendors served half a cup at a reduced price, though accounts differ. No reliable date or first vendor is documented.

The term has since become part of the city's identity: a Mumbai college media festival, running since 2007, takes its name from the drink.
